plain: Colorado now taxes the taxable income of people and businesses at one rate, 4.4 percent. Amendment 87 would switch to six brackets, with lower rates on the first $100,000 and higher rates above $500,000.
agree_means: Agreeing means backing Amendment 87. Most filers pay a little less, people with taxable income over $500,000 pay more, and about $2 billion a year goes to schools, health care and child care.
disagree_means: Disagreeing means keeping the flat 4.4 percent rate. No one’s state income tax changes, and the state does not collect the extra money.

now.text: Colorado has taxed income at one flat rate since 1987, now 4.4 percent. It is one of 15 states with a flat income tax.

sources.title: 2026 Colorado State Ballot Information Booklet (Blue Book) (Legislative Council Staff)
sources.quote: Since 1987, Colorado has had a flat income tax rate, in which all taxpayers, including individuals and businesses, pay the same income tax rate on their income.

sources.quote: At 4.4%, Colorado is one of 15 states with a flat individual income tax rate.

now.text: Amendment 87 would start in 2027. Rates would run from 3.7 percent to 8.4 percent. The brackets would not rise with inflation.

sources.title: Colorado Voters Weigh a Tax Transformation (Governing)
sources.quote: under the proposed Amendment 87, which will appear on the state ballot this fall, Colorado would introduce a graduated, six-tier income tax ranging from 3.7 percent on income up to $25,000 to 8.4 percent on earnings over $1 million.

sources.title: 2026 Colorado State Ballot Information Booklet (Blue Book) (Legislative Council Staff)
sources.quote: Unlike the federal income tax, the new state income tax brackets are not adjusted for inflation, so more of taxpayers’ incomes will fall into the higher brackets over time.

now.text: Legislative Council economists say the 2027-28 budget could end $315.4 million below the required reserve once rising costs are counted. Two 2025 studies said schools need $3.5 to $4.1 billion more each year.

research_notes: No source in this file needed the browser; the Chrome extension was not connected, so the one browser-pane session I used was for CBO pages in the federal-budget-law file. Every quote was machine-checked against my saved copy of its page. For a reviewer: (1) Blue Book Table 3 rows used as quotes are PDF table text; the checker may extract table cells in a different order. Table 3 prints 408,912 taxpayers for both the $70,000-$99,999 and $100,000-$149,999 rows, which may be a Blue Book typo. (2) The 97 percent figure is the supporters' Blue Book argument. The Colorado Fiscal Institute says the official analysis shows it; I found no Legislative Council sentence stating it. (3) Migration evidence is split. The Common Sense Institute (free-market think tank) figures are its own model. The Colorado Fiscal Institute page is a coalition member's summary and is undated, so its date is the access day. The Stanford abstract is from 2016; the page shows month only, so the date is set to 2016-06-01. (4) The lawsuit over petition signatures was still pending in the latest coverage I found (Oct. 8); check for a ruling. (5) I avoided counts of graduated-tax states because sources differ (26 vs 27). (6) The web search budget ran out before I could look for more independent economic analysis.
